post_text:
We split our high-throughput ledger into separate read and write models using basic database views instead of an event-sourced CQRS framework.

Everyone else wanted to deploy Kafka and a NoSQL read store to handle the projected scale.

I fought hard for simple SQL views and a separate read-only replica, but the team called it outdated.

I spent nights worrying that my conservative approach would bottleneck the launch and prove my critics right.

We were building a core financial ledger, and the pressure to use a modern, event-driven stack was immense.

Two quarters later, a marketing campaign triggered a 50x spike in read traffic while write patterns remained steady.

While our competitors' complex event-driven systems struggled with eventual consistency lags, our database replica handled the read load effortlessly.

We scaled the read-only instances in minutes without losing a single transaction.

Choosing boring database features over trendy distributed frameworks saved us months of operational troubleshooting.

It reminded me that logical separation does not require physical infrastructure complexity.

Almost nobody asks what happens next.

What I learned:

True architectural resilience often comes from pushing simple tools to their limits rather than introducing complex new systems prematurely.
